column1: The thesis titled International Vulnerability of Inflation by Ignacio Garrón  Vladimir Rodríguez-Caballero  and Esther Ruiz explores the increasing influence of international factors on domestic inflation in a globalized economy. The authors propose a methodology to measure inflation vulnerability using Inflation-at-risk and Deflation-at-risk metrics  derived from factor-augmented quantile regressions. These regressions incorporate international factors extracted from a multi-level Dynamic Factor Model  which groups economies by geographical region or development level. The study analyzes monthly inflation data from 1999 to 2022 across over 115 countries.

The findings indicate that in many developed countries  international factors significantly impact the upper tail of the inflation distribution  suggesting a greater vulnerability to high inflation rather than average or low inflation. Conversely  inflation in developing low-income countries appears less affected by international conditions  while middle-income countries show mixed results. The study also highlights that the predictive power of international factors has increased in recent years  particularly during periods of high inflation.

The research underscores the importance for policymakers to understand international influences on domestic inflation  as ignoring these factors could lead to overestimating domestic inflation and misguiding macroeconomic policies. The paper contributes to the ongoing debate about the role of globalization in domestic inflation dynamics  emphasizing the need for a comprehensive approach that considers both domestic and international factors in inflation modeling and forecasting.
